source: Lieder & Griffiths (2015) When to use which heuristic: A rational solution to the strategy selection problem (CogSci)
finding: Core recipe for learned strategy selection. For each strategy, learn to predict its expected reward and its run time from cheap features of the problem. Pick the strategy with the best predicted reward minus time cost (value of computation). Learn the predictions by Bayesian linear or logistic regression. Explore with Thompson sampling: pick each strategy with the probability that its value is the highest.
numbers: VOC(s;i) ~ E[R|s,i] - E[TC(T)|s,i]; s* = argmax over strategies. Five hand-made features for risky choice; ten strategies from Payne et al. 1988.
quote: people learn a mental model that enables them to predict each heuristic's accuracy and execution time from features of the problem
limits: Features were chosen by hand, not learned. Tested on binary decisions and risky choice, not on open-ended reasoning. Simulation fits, not a controlled human learning curve.
agent_relevance: This is directly codeable as the S0 gate: a table or small regression per operator, predicting gain and token cost from problem features, with Thompson sampling for unknown operators. No model judgment is needed.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2015) When to use which heuristic: A rational solution to the strategy selection problem (CogSci)
finding: Context-free learners (SSL, RELACS) learn one average value per strategy, so they collapse to one habit when problems are mixed. Feature-based rational metareasoning keeps choosing the right strategy per problem.
numbers: Simulation over 11 environments: when the share of compensatory problems nears 50/50, SSL and RELACS fall to chance (50%); rational metareasoning stays above 70%. In homogeneous environments SSL and rational metareasoning perform equally.
limits: Simulated agents with hand-set parameters, 1000 simulations per cell.
agent_relevance: A per-operator running average (a context-free bandit) fails on mixed problem streams. The scaffold needs a feature-conditioned estimate, since our task mix is heterogeneous.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2015) When to use which heuristic: A rational solution to the strategy selection problem (CogSci)
finding: New human experiment in a mixed environment where Take-the-Best and weighted-additive always disagree. People beat chance, which context-free learning cannot explain, but they did not show learning over 30 trials.
numbers: 120 MTurk participants, 30 binary loan decisions. Mean accuracy 64.6% (99% credible interval 62.5% to 66.6%) vs 50% for any fixed or context-free strategy. Slope of improvement 95% CI [-0.1%, 0.2%] per trial: no significant learning. People did worse on non-compensatory than compensatory trials.
limits: Only 30 trials, stochastic feedback, complex environment. Authors say absence of learning is not evidence against it. Could also be one complex strategy that works on both kinds of problems.
agent_relevance: Humans start with decent strategy-selection skill and learn slowly. Our agent should ship with a prior table (from past logs) instead of learning every cue online.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2015) When to use which heuristic: A rational solution to the strategy selection problem (CogSci)
finding: The model reproduces Payne et al. (1988) adaptivity without feedback: more selective, attribute-based processing under time pressure and under high dispersion of outcome probabilities. SSL and RELACS predict no difference between the four conditions.
numbers: Simulated Payne et al. 1988 Exp 1: 4 problem types (15 s limit vs none; low vs high dispersion), 10 problems each, 10 strategies, 1 s per elementary operation.
limits: Simulation of someone else's published result, not a new human sample. Time cost was assumed to be 1 s per operation.
agent_relevance: A budget limit should change which operator is picked even with no feedback: cost enters the choice directly. Our S0 gate should shift to cheap operators as the remaining budget shrinks.

source: Callaway, Lieder, Das, Gul, Krueger & Griffiths (2018) A resource-rational analysis of human planning (CogSci)
finding: Older computational system built on the framework. The optimal planning strategy is computed as a metalevel decision problem (each click is a costly computation). It predicts the order of human clicks better than breadth-first, depth-first and other planning models.
numbers: Exp 1: 60 MTurk participants recruited (15% excluded for not following instructions). Participants followed best-first search 82.1% of the time. About 45.0% of the computations were as the optimal strategy chooses. 28.3% of deviations were from stopping too early; 6.3% from planning too long.
limits: Mouselab-style process tracing; an artificial route-planning task. Systematic deviations remain (e.g. continued exploring other first actions 57.0% of the time).
agent_relevance: Shows how to derive a stopping and search rule from a cost model and test it against traces. Our agent's stopping rule can be derived the same way and checked against logged runs.

source: Callaway, Lieder, Das, Gul, Krueger & Griffiths (2018) A resource-rational analysis of human planning (CogSci)
finding: Experiment 2: environment structure shapes the strategy. With variance that grows with depth, people inspected end states first; with variance that shrinks, they did not.
numbers: First click inspected a potential end state 95.0% of the time in one condition vs 0.3% in the other. Resource-rational model BIC = 21203 (better than competing planning models).
limits: Small, artificial environments. Reward structure was taught to participants through a quiz.
agent_relevance: Cue-to-strategy rules depend on reward variance by depth. A cheap feature such as 'how informative is a partial attempt' can choose between forward and backward search.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut & Griffiths (2024/2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models
finding: First direct use of the Lieder-Griffiths value-of-computation idea to train an LLM. Reward of a reasoning chain = utility minus cost. Utility is the gain in log-probability of the target answer from adding the chain. Cost is proportional to chain length. Trained by expert iteration (keep the best chain per question by this reward, fine-tune).
numbers: R(x,y,z) = U(z|x,y) - lambda*len(z); U = log pi(y|z,x) - log pi(y|x). Models: Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B (base and instruct). Data: ARC, CommonsenseQA, GSM8K, ProofWriter; MMLU-CF held out.
limits: Needs fine-tuning and a gold answer to compute utility. Cannot be used as is in a scaffold without training. The utility is the model's own likelihood, so it inherits its calibration.
agent_relevance: Gives a scaffold-level analogue: estimate value of an operator as the change in a code-checkable score before and after, minus a token price. We cannot train, but we can log this reward per operator and use it as the S0 table.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut & Griffiths (2024/2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models
finding: Training on the cost-aware reward cut tokens while matching or raising accuracy. The reduction figures changed between arXiv versions.
numbers: v3 abstract: 23-45% fewer tokens across three models. Text: 35-42% fewer than few-shot CoT, 23-32% fewer than STaR, on average over the in-domain datasets. (v1 reported 20-37%.)
limits: Preprint, under review. Averages over datasets hide that chains mainly help on maths and logic, not on knowledge tasks (agrees with a meta-analysis of 100+ papers cited in the paper).
agent_relevance: Do not plan on a fixed saving. Expect 20-40% fewer tokens only where chains are not needed.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut & Griffiths (2024/2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models
finding: The cost-aware model is adaptive, not just shorter: it writes shorter chains on easy items than on hard ones, and more so than STaR. Instruction-tuned CoT is not adaptive at all.
numbers: Table 2 (hard vs easy split, mean tokens): Llama-3.2-3B RaM 145 vs 72 (50.3% length reduction on easy); STaR 195 vs 128 (34.4%); CoT few-shot 210 vs 170 (19.0%); CoT prompting on instruct 222 vs 221 (0.5%). Llama-3.1-8B RaM 139 vs 89 (36.0%); instruct CoT 228 vs 226 (0.9%).
limits: 'Easy' means direct few-shot answered correctly, which is a proxy for difficulty, not an independent measure.
agent_relevance: Plain 'think step by step' prompting gives no difficulty adaptation (0.5-0.9%). Adaptation must come from outside the model (code), which supports the design rule that the program, not the model, decides.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut & Griffiths (2024/2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models
finding: Out-of-domain test: fewer tokens, but accuracy is not always kept. Reasoning-heavy subjects (physics, engineering) saw smaller reductions.
numbers: MMLU-CF vs STaR: Llama-3.2-3B accuracy 27.0 -> 29.5, output tokens 150.6 -> 96.3; Llama-3.1-8B accuracy 40.2 -> 36.4 (a drop), output tokens 153.6 -> 110.6. About 28-36% fewer output tokens.
limits: Confidence intervals of about +/-2.4 points overlap, so the 8B drop is a possible small loss, not proven.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: cost cutting can lose a few accuracy points out of domain. Keep a safety floor so the gate never removes a step that a check says is needed.

source: Hu, Roshan & Varma (2026) Are More Tokens Rational? Inference-Time Scaling in Language Models as Adaptive Resource Rationality
finding: Closest LLM test of strategy selection in the Lieder-Griffiths sense. In a Variable Attribution Task, reasoning models and instruct models both shift from trying pairs one by one (permutation) to pruning the candidate set (elimination) as the hypothesis space grows.
numbers: 3000 items, 10 Boolean functions, N in {3..16} candidate variables, T = Tmin + 0..5 trials, 5 samples per cell. Models: DeepSeek R1 and V3, Qwen3-Next-80B Thinking and Instruct. Strategy labelled by Kimi-K2 judge: accuracy 0.86, Cohen's kappa 0.76 on 100 human-labelled items.
quote: resource rationality is an emergent property of inference-time scaling itself
limits: Strategy labels come from an LLM judge. Only two model families. No human data collected, so 'human-like' is not tested. Authors admit longer traces may reflect attention limits rather than deliberate allocation.
agent_relevance: Models do change strategy with problem size on their own, so a cheap size feature (candidate count) is a valid cue for an S0 table. Measure it for our own backbone before relying on it.

source: Hu, Roshan & Varma (2026) Are More Tokens Rational? Inference-Time Scaling in Language Models as Adaptive Resource Rationality
finding: Strategy choice follows a cost-benefit rule. Elimination is chosen more when the hypothesis space is large and less when more trials are given; for XOR/XNOR (where pruning helps little) Qwen almost never switches.
numbers: Logistic regression with interaction: beta(log hypothesis-space size) = +1.0212, beta(trials) = -0.1466, both p < .001; AIC 2727.29, pseudo R2 = 0.160 (weak fit, most variance unexplained).
limits: Pseudo R2 of 0.16 means size and trials explain a small part of the choice. Not a test that the chosen strategy was the best one.
agent_relevance: A two-feature logistic gate is a reasonable first form of the table, but expect a low ceiling; always keep a fallback when the gate is unsure.

source: Hu, Roshan & Varma (2026) Are More Tokens Rational? Inference-Time Scaling in Language Models as Adaptive Resource Rationality
finding: Effort scales with difficulty and reasoning mode matters for accuracy. Reasoning models stay near-perfect across functions; instruct models degrade on XOR/XNOR as N grows; direct answering fails almost at once.
numbers: Character count grows linearly with N and T; XOR/XNOR have higher intercept and steeper slope. Direct-answer baseline for DeepSeek V3 approaches chance or zero accuracy as N grows.
limits: Accuracy shown mainly in figures (no exact table values read).
agent_relevance: Spending tokens is not wasted when the task needs working memory; a gate must not cut computation below the level a task class needs.

source: Yang, Hou, Wei, Bao & Chang (2026) ARES: Adaptive Reasoning Effort Selection for Efficient LLM Agents
finding: A small trained router picks low, medium or high reasoning effort at every agent step from the interaction history. It nearly keeps high-effort success with far fewer reasoning tokens. Fixed low effort and random choice both fail.
numbers: Backbone gpt-oss-20b. TAU-Bench Retail success: Low 35.0, Medium 47.3, High 54.8, Random 43.5, GPT-5 as router 40.0, Gemini-3-Pro router 46.1, ARES 54.8. Up to 52.7% fewer reasoning tokens than fixed high on TAU-Bench. BrowseComp-Plus: ARES 41.3 vs High 42.7 with 41.8% fewer tokens (Low 8.0). WebArena: ARES 46.5 vs High 45.0.
limits: Router is a fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B, trained per setting from logged trajectories. Gain over fixed high on WebArena is small (single runs, small test sets). Retail table columns read from jumbled extraction; main values match the text.
agent_relevance: Per-step effort gating from history works when trained on logs, and big LLMs asked to route (GPT-5, Gemini-3-Pro) did worse than the small trained router. Supports a code or small-model gate over asking the main model.

source: Yang, Hou, Wei, Bao & Chang (2026) ARES: Adaptive Reasoning Effort Selection for Efficient LLM Agents
finding: Ablations: the training data and the rationale step matter. An untrained Qwen3-1.7B router loses 13 points. Predicting the label without a short rationale loses 3.5 points.
numbers: Retail: ARES 54.8 -> 41.7 with no fine-tuning; -3.5 points without rationale. Labels come from the cheapest effort level that still gets the step right (K=3 trials per step).
limits: Single benchmark for ablations. The 'cheapest sufficient level' label needs ground-truth action sequences, which many tasks lack.
agent_relevance: The cheapest-sufficient-level labelling is a usable recipe for building our own S0 table from past runs: for each task class, find the cheapest operator or effort that still passed the check.

source: Yang, Hou, Wei, Bao & Chang (2026) ARES: Adaptive Reasoning Effort Selection for Efficient LLM Agents
finding: More thinking can hurt. In TAU-Bench Airline, high effort lost to medium. Reinforcement learning on the router, with a cost penalty, improved both success and cost.
numbers: Airline success: High 38.0, Medium 42.0. RL router: Airline 36.0 -> 42.0 and tokens 678k -> 133k (vs 873k for fixed high); Retail 54.8 -> 58.5 with 176k fewer tokens (476k vs 1007k for fixed high).
limits: Small test sets (Airline success values are multiples of 2 points, so about 50 tasks). Differences of 2-4 points are within noise.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that extra reasoning is not free of harm: the gate should include 'do not think more' as an option, with a measured benefit.

source: Yang, Hou, Wei, Bao & Chang (2026) ARES: Adaptive Reasoning Effort Selection for Efficient LLM Agents
finding: What the router learns looks like what metareasoning theory predicts: low effort at the first steps (simple navigation), more high effort later, and most high effort at recovery actions (go back, branch).
numbers: WebArena effort distribution by step index and action type (figures, no exact table). Early steps 0-2 mostly low effort.
limits: Descriptive only, read from figures and text.
agent_relevance: Cheap step features (step index, action type, just-failed) are valid inputs to an operator gate. Failure and backtrack steps are where to spend.

source: Sui, He, Cao, Han, Chen & Hooi (2025/2026) Meta-Reasoner: Dynamic Guidance for Optimized Inference-time Reasoning in LLMs
finding: A strategy-level bandit inside an LLM reasoning loop, in the spirit of rational strategy selection. Loop: the LLM writes a reasoning step, a progress report summarizes it, a LinUCB contextual bandit picks the next strategy (backtrack, simplify, verify, reset, clarify). Reward = progress score minus a step-count cost.
numbers: Reward: progress Sp = w1*correctness + w2*adherence, resource Ru = -lambda*Ns (steps). Game of 24: GPT-4o-mini 89, GPT-4o 92, vs ToT(b=5) 65, MACM 80, CoT 4. TheoremQA GPT-4o-mini 84.13 vs MACM with GPT-4 Turbo 79.41.
limits: Progress and correctness are scored by an LLM inside the loop, which conflicts with a code-only judge rule. Many baselines are from older papers with different setups. Numbers differ across arXiv versions (v6 in 2026).
agent_relevance: Same shape as our S0 gate, but our reward must come from code checks only. The bandit part is the transferable piece.

source: Sui, He, Cao, Han, Chen & Hooi (2025/2026) Meta-Reasoner: Dynamic Guidance for Optimized Inference-time Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Ablation shows the bandit beats letting the LLM choose its own strategy. Direct LLM arm selection is weaker, and on TheoremQA it drops close to plain CoT.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini: Game of 24 full 89, no progress report 85, direct LLM arm selection 82; TheoremQA full 84.13, no report about 79-80, direct selection about 39-40 (as extracted, close to CoT 39.46). Gemini-Exp-1206 Game of 24 full 94 vs direct 87. LinUCB cumulative reward beat both direct LLM choice and random.
limits: Table text was extracted in a jumbled order, so some TheoremQA cells may be misread. Few tasks, mostly maths puzzles.
agent_relevance: Evidence for 'code picks the strategy, the model does not': direct LLM selection was the weaker arm in every comparison given.

source: Liu, Zhou, Xu, Huang, Wang, Zhang, Poon & Chen (2025) MetaScale: Test-Time Scaling with Evolving Meta-Thoughts
finding: Pool of 'meta-thoughts' (how to think about this task type), chosen per question by UCB, with a genetic step that rewrites good ones. Improves win rate and accuracy over CoT and best-of-N, but rewards come from an LLM judge.
numbers: Arena-Hard win rate, GPT-4o: vanilla 82.14, CoT 84.72, best-of-N w/ CoT 87.42, MetaScale w/o evolution 89.63, MetaScale 93.14 (tokens 573 -> 699). Llama-3.1-8B: 18.94 vanilla, 12.50 CoT, 30.86 MetaScale.
limits: Reward is an LLM judge (the type of scoring our guardrails distrust). Arena-Hard is judged by GPT-4 Turbo, so style gains are possible. Small MMLU-Pro/GSM8K samples (accuracy steps of 1.56 points = 64 items).
agent_relevance: Shows that a learned choice among ways of thinking helps, and that CoT can hurt a small model (Llama 12.50 vs 18.94). The bandit works; the judge reward is the weak link.

source: Zhang, Wisniewski, Tomeh & Charnois (2025) Reasoning Strategies in LLMs: Can They Follow, Prefer, and Optimize?
finding: When models are told to use a named strategy (supposition following, chain construction, compositional, concatenation), no strategy beats letting the model pick. Models cannot choose the best strategy per item, but an oracle that could would gain a lot.
numbers: Phi-4 TruthQuest: no strategy 47.2%, strategies 45.1-49.0%, oracle over strategies 82.9%. R1-Distill TruthQuest: 63.4% vs oracle 90.1%. ZebraLogic Phi-4 27.3% vs oracle 37.7%; Qwen3 32.0% vs 36.4%.
limits: Logic puzzles only. The oracle is an upper bound that picks per item after the fact and is inflated by noise: best of 4 noisy runs would score higher even if strategies were equal.
agent_relevance: The oracle gap is partly lucky-sample selection (G4). Real headroom for strategy choice is smaller than 82.9 vs 47.2. Test any gate against a random-choice control, not only against the oracle.

source: Zhang, Wisniewski, Tomeh & Charnois (2025) Reasoning Strategies in LLMs: Can They Follow, Prefer, and Optimize?
finding: Post-hoc selection among strategy outputs recovers a part of the gap, but no rule wins everywhere: majority vote, max probability, min entropy and an LLM verifier each win somewhere.
numbers: Phi-4 TruthQuest: majority vote 54.9, min entropy 48.8, max prob 48.4, verifier 46.9, vote+prob 57.3, vote+verifier 55.8. R1-Distill TruthQuest: verifier 74.1, vote 68.4. ZebraLogic gains small (27.9 / 28.2 vs 27.3).
limits: Gains from voting come in part from averaging noise. Authors note no merging rule is consistently best.
agent_relevance: Majority vote across strategies is cheap but only a hint (G4). A verifier helped most for the reasoning model on TruthQuest; verifiers still need an external check.

source: Li, Huang, Guo, Wang & Zhang (2026) Same Signal, Opposite Meaning: Direction-Informed Adaptive Learning for LLM Agents (DIAL)
finding: Key warning for any cue-based gate. The sign of the link between an uncertainty cue (token entropy) and the benefit of extra compute flips across environments and across backbones. High uncertainty can mean extra rollouts hurt. The classic assumption that value of computation is at least zero fails for agents.
numbers: Spearman(entropy, utility of rollout): HotpotQA Qwen3 -0.327, Phi-3.5 +0.184, Llama-3.1 -0.346; WebShop +0.133, +0.335, +0.287; FEVER -0.119, -0.156, +0.428; APPS +0.317, -0.024, -0.249. Fixed-direction assumption violated on half of six environments.
quote: the same signal predicts rollout benefit in one setting and rollout harm in another
limits: Utility estimated from counterfactual rollouts in six environments with three open backbones; correlations are modest. Entropy is the main cue tested.
agent_relevance: A gate trained on one task class or one model cannot be moved to another without re-fitting. The S0 table must be fitted per backbone and per class from our own logs, and must allow a negative value.

source: Li, Huang, Guo, Wang & Zhang (2026) Same Signal, Opposite Meaning: Direction-Informed Adaptive Learning for LLM Agents (DIAL)
finding: Fix: learn the direction of each cue's effect per (environment, backbone) from counterfactual runs with and without the extra compute, then use a sparse gate. Fewer rollouts can even raise success.
numbers: DIAL has the highest success rate in 16 of 18 (environment, backbone) cells. Example cell: base only 37.0%, always-trigger 59.8%, DIAL 49.8% (falls short of always). WebShop DIAL 57.3%.
limits: Gate trained on counterfactual data that costs extra runs. In some cells always-trigger is still much better, so cost saving is not free.
agent_relevance: The right training data for an S0 gate is paired runs (operator on vs off) on the same item; this matches the metareasoning view that value is a difference, not a level.

source: Zhang, Zhang, Xiang & Cai (2026) Reasoning Is Not Free: Robust Adaptive Cost-Efficient Routing for LLM-as-a-Judge (RACER)
finding: Reasoning mode helps a judge mostly on math and code (verification tasks) and can hurt on safety and knowledge items. So reasoning should be switched on selectively, with a router robust to distribution shift.
numbers: Qwen3 1.7B/4B/8B hybrid models, reasoning vs non-reasoning mode, on JudgeBench, RewardBench, RewardBench 2. Case analysis: reasoning helps with explicit verification, is redundant when surface cues decide, and hurts when it widens the evaluation scope.
limits: Judge accuracy gains read from figures; exact deltas per domain not extracted. Distribution-shift router is theory-heavy.
agent_relevance: A domain feature (verification-heavy vs recall) is a real cue for whether thinking pays, in agreement with the RaM boundary result.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) RACER, appendix on self-routing
finding: When the model itself is asked whether to use reasoning mode, it says yes almost always. Self-routing is not a gate.
numbers: Qwen3 reasoning fraction under self-routing: 1.7B 99.91%, 4B 99.51%, 8B 99.88%. Accuracy: all-instruct 70.04 / 81.96 / 82.20; self-routing 78.34 / 86.50 / 87.86; cost ratio 19.07 / 6.25 / 6.36 times the instruct cost.
limits: One model family, one judge task. Accuracy under self-routing is close to all-reasoning accuracy because it nearly always chooses reasoning.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for the rule that the program, not the model, decides how much to think: the model picks the expensive option about 99.5-99.9% of the time.

source: Xue, Lou, Xing & Huang (2026) R2-Router: A New Paradigm for LLM Routing with Reasoning (ICML 2026)
finding: Routing is on a quality-versus-length curve, not a point: the router jointly picks the model and an output-length budget, enforced by 'use at most K tokens'. This is the 'how much to compute' side of metareasoning, done by a router.
numbers: 4-5x lower cost than prior routers at equal quality. OOD queries: AUDC 0.71 vs 0.67 for the best baseline. Oracle on the new R2-Bench: AUDC 0.85 -> 0.98, normalized cost QNC 0.18 -> 0.04. Expanded pool: AUDC 0.623 vs 0.590, QNC down 80%. Data: over 405k outputs from 11 LLMs.
limits: Length control by prompt instruction; compliance varies by model (large models comply reliably, small ones less). Quality judged by LLM judges.
agent_relevance: Output-length budget is a controllable operator parameter. The S0 table should store gain per token budget, not one value per operator.

source: Sheikhi (2026) Chain of Simulation: A Dual-Mode Reasoning Framework with Dynamic Problem Routing
finding: Weak evidence: a three-mode router sending problems to different reasoning modes. Shows that a wrong mode can fail completely, but the test sets are tiny.
numbers: GSM8K 71.5% (+1.0 point over best baseline), StrategyQA 90.0% (+2.5), bAbI 19.0%. Computational mode on routed math: 81.2% (n=176); symbolic mode on math: 0.0%. Mode misclassification caused 12% of errors.
limits: Samples of only 50 problems per benchmark per model; differences of 1-2.5 points are inside noise. Single author, preprint.
agent_relevance: Misrouting cost can be total (0%), so the gate needs a safe default and a check after the step, not a bare classifier.

source: Oh (2025) Before you think, monitor: Implementing Flavell's metacognitive framework in LLMs
finding: Weak evidence: selecting a strategy up front (monitor, then generate, then verify) beat self-refine and self-verification on GSM8K, with fewer attempts but 27-37% more time.
numbers: GSM8K, 659 problems: MGV 75.42% (497/659), Self-REFINE 68.44% (451/659), Self-Verification 67.07% (442/659). Attempts 1.3 vs 2.0 vs 1.2. Time 9.60 s vs 6.98 s vs 7.52 s.
limits: Single model, arithmetic only, single run, preliminary workshop report. Strategy knowledge base was built with gpt-4-0613.
agent_relevance: Up-front strategy choice plus a check is plausible but unproven. Treat as a hint only.

source: Paglieri et al. (2025) Learning When to Plan: Efficiently Allocating Test-Time Compute for LLM Agents
finding: Abstract only. Agents that plan before every action (ReAct-style) waste compute and do worse on long tasks; never planning also limits them. A trained dynamic-planning agent decides when to plan; it is more sample-efficient in Crafter.
numbers: No figures read; abstract names only the Crafter environment.
limits: Full paper not opened (PDF download was damaged). Two-stage training (SFT then RL) needed.
agent_relevance: Supports 'doubt on a signal, not on a schedule' (G1) in the compute-allocation form.

source: Qian et al. (2025) xRouter: Training Cost-Aware LLMs Orchestration System via Reinforcement Learning
finding: Abstract only. A tool-calling router answers directly or calls other models, trained by RL with a cost-aware reward; reports large cost cuts at similar completion rates and notes that small open models find sophisticated orchestration hard to learn.
numbers: No figures read (PDF was damaged on download; only the abstract page was read).
limits: Not opened beyond abstract.
agent_relevance: Reminds that a learned router needs enough data; for a scaffold with few logs a hand-set table with Thompson sampling is the safer start.

source: Callaway et al. (2022) Rational use of cognitive resources in human planning (Nature Human Behaviour 6, 1112-1125)
finding: Abstract-level result from search: heuristics such as best-first search are near-optimal in some environments but not others, people adapt planning to each environment, and no single heuristic model fits; systematic departures from the optimal model remain.
numbers: No numbers read this session.
limits: Journal article not opened; the 2018 conference version was opened instead.
agent_relevance: Cited as the journal-level test of the resource-rational planning model.

source: Search note: no LLM-on-Mouselab or strategy-selection-learning study found
finding: Searches found no paper that runs an LLM through Mouselab, strategy-selection-learning (Rieskamp and Otto style), or sorting-algorithm selection paradigms against human data. Hu et al. 2026 is the nearest. A 2026 Springer study reportedly finds a greedy metalevel model only partly explains information search in a chatbot Mouselab; Glockner and Betsch argue Mouselab restricts search itself.
numbers: Search result only; none of these were opened.
limits: Absence in a few searches is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: An open gap: nobody has tested whether an LLM learns strategy-by-feature selection from outcome feedback. Our own logs could be the first test.
